background_notes.fact: A compact C⊂ℝ^n is closed and bounded. There is R>0 with C⊂(−R,R)^n, also when C is empty; its complement is open.

grounds.reason: n is a finite positive integer.
F001 supplies a compact subset C of ℝ^n; S002 chooses it.

background_notes.justification: Euclidean space is Hausdorff, so its compact subsets are closed. The increasing cover by balls of positive integer radii has a finite subcover of C, giving a norm bound; each coordinate's absolute value is at most the Euclidean norm. Increase that bound strictly and take it positive to obtain R. For empty C any positive R works. These are routine compactness consequences at the point explicitly used in S002.

background_notes.fact: For a smooth u:ℝ^n×(0,∞)→ℝ^m, all its coordinate derivatives are smooth; finite sums, products and inner products of these derivatives are smooth. In particular e and e_t are smooth, with e_t=2u_t·u_tt+2Σ_{j=1}^n ∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t. If u=q on the open set (ℝ^n\C)×int J, every positive-order mixed space/time derivative vanishes there. Each spatial function listed in F005 is continuous and has support contained in C for fixed r∈int J.

grounds.reason: Joint smoothness on the open positive-time domain is H002.
Coordinate derivatives and inner products are componentwise Euclidean operations.
e is the stated finite sum of derivative squares.
C is closed and u=q on the open exterior times int J, by F001.

background_notes.justification: Repeated differentiation preserves smoothness, and the finite product rule gives the displayed expression; smoothness allows interchange of the mixed derivatives. Locally u is constant on the stated open set, so its first derivatives vanish and iteration gives vanishing of every positive-order mixed derivative. The listed products and their differentiated products therefore vanish outside C at the indicated times. Smoothness implies continuity of each slice, and since C is closed, the closure of each nonzero set is still contained in C.

background_notes.fact: For finite n and R>0, Q=[−R,R]^n is compact and Lebesgue measurable, with measure (2R)^n<∞. If a real continuous f on ℝ^n vanishes outside a closed C⊂Q, then f is bounded on Q, measurable and absolutely integrable: for some finite M≥0, |f|≤M 1_Q and ∫|f|≤M(2R)^n.

grounds.reason: dx is standard Lebesgue measure, with the stated rectangle product normalization.
F002 gives positive finite R and C inside the open box.
S003 chooses R and Q and derives continuity and vanishing outside C for every listed slice.

background_notes.justification: Closed bounded intervals are compact and their finite product Q is compact; the product rectangle measure is the product of side lengths 2R. A continuous real function is Borel measurable, hence Lebesgue measurable. On compact Q continuity gives a finite absolute bound (a finite subcover of neighborhoods on which |f| is locally bounded suffices). Outside Q, f=0. The measurable function M1_Q has finite integral M|Q|; monotonicity of the nonnegative Lebesgue integral yields the displayed bound and absolute integrability. This applies separately to each indicated r and j; no common slice bound is required here.

background_notes.fact: With t0>0, η=t0/4 and Q=[−R,R]^n for R>0, K=Q×[t0−η,t0+η] is a nonempty compact subset of ℝ^n×(0,∞). If e_t is continuous on that domain, there exists B≥0 with |e_t|≤B on K.

grounds.reason: Q is the compact box with R>0, and e_t is smooth.
The endpoints are 3t0/4 and 5t0/4 and the entire interval lies in int J.

background_notes.justification: The closed time interval is nonempty and compact with positive endpoints. Q is nonempty because it contains zero, and finite products of compact sets are compact. Absolute value composed with continuous e_t is continuous. A finite subcover of local neighborhoods where its values are bounded gives a finite bound on K; increasing that bound to a nonnegative number gives B. The bound is simultaneous in x and r, as required.
